title: From Retrofit to Native Accessibility: User-Driven Requirement Engineering and Inventive Design of a Non-Medicalised Car for Wheelchair Users
content: Wheelchair-accessible vehicles are commonly developed by modifying conventional platforms, introducing functional and aesthetic compromises. This study presents a user-centred engineering approach to designing a natively accessible passenger car with a non-medicalised identity. A questionnaire involving 100 stakeholders informed the identification of ten user requirements, prioritised through pairwise comparison and interdependence analysis. Six commercial wheelchair-accessible configurations were evaluated through technical benchmarking and Top-Flop analysis. Quality Function Deployment (QFD), the Kano model, TRIZ, and morphological analysis guided the translation of requirements into design solutions. Universal Accessibility and Adaptability received the highest importance weights (12% each), while Adaptability and Ease of Access showed the strongest interdependence. The Peugeot Rifter Horizon L2 RS achieved the highest Top-Flop balance (Δ = +2). QFD identified steering-wheel hand controls, access-system configuration, and interior reconfigurability as the leading technical priorities, with normalised scores of 10.00, 9.18, and 8.66, respectively. These priorities informed EVERY, an electric crossover concept integrating a pedal-free steering interface, a reconfigurable tunnel-free cabin, and an automated side-access platform. The resulting design framework connects stakeholder needs, engineering priorities, and vehicle architecture.
